C4 REPLAY ── SEVENTEEN TURNS

One campaign, played end to end against a live LLM backend. Briefings arrive, the cabinet is questioned in plain English, the Prime Minister writes a paragraph, and the game makes the world answer it.

It starts with a Russian submarine surfacing off Orkney and two dead F-35 pilots in Norfolk. By turn seventeen the Prime Minister is no longer investigating an attack on Britain but hunting a service that wears other countries' faces. Nothing in that arc was scripted; it is what the adjudicator made of seventeen paragraphs of free text.

A shorter campaign, spent finding the edge of the system →

How to read this. Every pane below is the real terminal output, colour and box-drawing intact. Captures were recorded with piped input, so the terminal never echoed the Prime Minister's typing — those lines have been put back from the recorded input files and are shown in amber. Nothing else is added, reordered or rewritten; only the repeated title sequence at the top of each resumed turn, the rate-limit chatter, and the empty >: echoes the piped-play scaffold left behind when it stepped through a pacing gate — which a player at a keyboard never sees — have been dropped.

The Barents Sea lies black and restless beneath a thin crescent moon. At the mouth of 
Kola Bay, the silhouettes of seven ballistic missile submarines slip silently from their 
moorings, one after another, like great whales departing into the deep.

Their conning towers cut dark shapes against the receding cliffs of the Kola Peninsula. 
Choppy waves catch fragments of moonlight, breaking silver against the submarines' hulls 
before they submerge. Within minutes, only roiling wakes mark their passage.

On the pier, a lone figure watches through night-vision binoculars. Emerging from the 
shadows of the coastline, the entire Northern Fleet drives silently towards a sleeping 
United Kingdom. The largest submarine force Russia has sent to sea since the Cold War 
carries out its orders — the first, unalterable act of Operation Tuman.

Operation Tuman — "Fog" — has begun.

Deep beneath Northwood Headquarters, the Joint Operations Centre hums with controlled 
urgency. Wall-sized displays show the North Atlantic in real-time: blue icons for Allied 
forces, red for Russian. The red icons have multiplied dramatically in the past 72 hours.

A Royal Navy commander briefs the duty officer: "Fifteen submarines, sir. Seven SSBNs, 
eight SSNs. Plus surface escorts. They're forming up southwest of Iceland, heading 
toward the GIUK gap."

"Fifteen?" The duty officer's voice is tight. "When did we last see numbers like this?"

"Never, sir. Not in peacetime. Not even during the Cold War."

The commander pauses, then adds quietly: "And that's just what we can track."

A secure phone rings. The duty officer answers, listens, then sets it down carefully.

"Get COBRA on the line. The Prime Minister needs to see this. Now."

The air is thick with tension. No one speaks as you enter. They're waiting for you.

• THE NATIONAL SECURITY ADVISOR sits to your right, leaning forward with hands

Decision>: Two answers today, one for each signal. The submarine: the Royal Navy escorts the Akula 
out with complete professionalism and open cameras - we publish our own footage before Moscow 
publishes theirs, because whoever narrates first owns the incident, and a show of force answered 
with seamanship is a show wasted. The offer: we accept the joint investigation - on terms. The 
wreckage remains on British soil under British chain of custody; examination proceeds with Russian 
technical experts present alongside international observers - Poland for the alliance, Ireland as 
the neutral chair, given Dublin has already opened its ports to this operation. Every session 
documented, every finding shared simultaneously with NATO. If Moscow's offer was genuine, we have 
just built the room where the third hand gets found; if it was a trap, they must now refuse their 
own proposal in front of the world. Paris owes us an answer on the ambassador meeting by tonight - 
the Foreign Secretary collects it. And the forensics first-read still comes to this room before 
anyone

[Narrator] The hours tick by with agonizing slowness, the only sound in the dimly lit Situation Room
the soft hum of computer screens and the occasional rustle of papers as aides and advisors pour over
intelligence reports. Outside, a cold autumn mist creeps over Whitehall, shrouding the streets in a 
damp, impenetrable gloom that seems to mirror the growing sense of unease within the government. As 
the first light of dawn begins to seep into the sky, the room falls silent, all eyes fixed on the 
secure video conference link, waiting for the latest update from the joint investigation.


The Russian Akula-class submarine, escorted out of UK waters by the Royal Navy, has now retreated to
international waters. However, intelligence reports indicate that the submarine has transmitted 
encrypted messages to its command center, and satellite imagery suggests that additional Russian 
naval assets are moving into the region. The joint investigation into the Severomorsk incident and 
the missile launch has commenced, with Russian technical experts arriving in the UK to participate 
alongside international observers from Poland, Ireland, and France.

The investigation team has begun examining the wreckage of the missile, and preliminary findings 
suggest that the missile's guidance system was compromised, potentially indicating a cyber attack or
sabotage. The Russian technical experts have requested access to the missile's propulsion system, 
citing concerns about potential defects in the manufacturing process. The UK's intelligence agencies
are working to verify the authenticity of the Russian claims and assess the potential risks of 
sharing sensitive information.

Meanwhile, the UK's military commanders are weighing their options for responding to the Russian 
submarine's presence and the potential escalation of the crisis. The UK's Type-45 destroyer, HMS 
Defender, remains on station, monitoring the situation and providing a visible deterrent to further 
Russian aggression. The US has issued a statement reiterating its support for the UK's decision to 
accept the joint investigation, but has stopped short of committing to any further action.

Decision>: We hold the line and let the evidence arrive. No change in military posture, no forward 
deployment, no attribution - the examination reports or it does not, and until it does this 
government says only what it can prove. Three things move today. First, the pilots: the Security 
Service brings me the access list - every person who knew those men's identities and movements - and
I want it before the wreckage reads out, because if this house is leaking, the leak is older than 
the crisis. Second, the country: the daily sitreps continue, and I go to the House to state plainly 
that we have accused nobody, that the evidence table is convened with allies and adversary alike at 
it, and that this government will not spend British lives on a hypothesis. Third, the alliance: 
Poland, France, Ireland and the United States get the same paper at the same hour - no tiered 
briefing, no favourites - because the surest way to break this coalition is to let one ally learn 
something from another. And when the examination reports, whatever it says, this room hears it and 
acts on it within the day. No delay, no shading, no matter whose name is on it

nothing points a gun at anyone. Meanwhile the examination becomes my first priority: I want its 
interim finding within twenty-four hours, published simultaneously to all four capitals, however 
partial - and the Security Service access list on the murdered pilots on my desk tonight, whatever 
it says and whoever is on it

maintain a continuous watch on the area, and a survey vessel has been tasked to investigate the

serial numbers and propellant batch match those of a Russian-manufactured missile. However, the

>: Attorney General, if a Russian-built missile was fired at Britain under someone else's control, 
what does the law say I am entitled to do, and to whom
      ·       ·    ·     ·             ───●───·      •            •· ··  •    

  Attorney General

  International Law and Self-Defence

  As the Legal Advisor, I must emphasize that the situation described by
  the Prime Minister, where a Russian-built missile was fired at Britain
  under someone else's control, raises complex questions about
  self-defence, state responsibility, and
  international law.

  In this scenario, the UK may be entitled to take action in
  self-defence, as enshrined in Article 51 of the UN
  Charter. However, the threshold for self-defence is
  high, and any action taken must be proportionate and
  necessary to prevent further attacks.

  Key Factors: * Attribution: The UK must be
  able to attribute the attack to a specific state or non-state
  actor. * Imminence: The attack must be
  imminent or ongoing. * Necessity:
  The action taken must be necessary to prevent further
  attacks. * Proportionality: The action taken must be
  proportionate to the threat posed.

  In terms of who the UK is entitled to take action against,
  it would depend on the evidence and attributed
  responsibility. If the attack is attributed to a
  state, the UK may be entitled to take action against that
  state. However, if the attack is attributed to a non-state
  actor, the situation becomes more complex, and the UK may need to
  consider alternative options, such as working with the host
  state to take action against the non-state actor.

  → I RECOMMEND that the Prime Minister consult with
    the National Security Council and NATO allies to
    discuss the situation and potential responses, ensuring that any
    actions taken are consistent with international law and
    comply with the UK's legal obligations.

it and not one hour before

Decision>: We hunt the hand, not the flag. Three orders. First, the technical trail: GCHQ, the 
examination team and our allies' experts reconstruct the in-flight takeover - the command link used,
the frequencies, the position from which it had to be transmitted. A hijack in flight has a 
geometry; someone had to be somewhere with something. Find me the footprint. Second, the human 
trail: the pilots' case and the guidance breach merge into a single counter-intelligence 
investigation under the Security Service, reporting to me alone, with the working assumption that 
the leak is inside the British system - and I want it run by people whose access predates this 
crisis, because if our own house is penetrated then the investigators must be above the penetration.
Third, the ground: I speak to Moscow again on the open channel and tell them exactly what our 
engineers found, including the part that exonerates them, because two governments being played 
against each other is precisely what our adversary requires, and the cheapest way to defeat it is to
compare notes with the man I was supposed to be at war with. And to this room: from tonight, no 
intelligence relating to this investigation is shared with any partner service until we know how our
pilots were found. That includes our closest friends. I am sorry for it, and I will explain it to 
them myself

Decision>: If the overlap is real then we stop investigating two crimes and start hunting one 
adversary, and everything follows from that. The joint cell's comparison becomes the priority 
intelligence requirement of this government: I want the author's profile - tooling, tradecraft, 
language, timezone, the shape of their mistakes - and I want it built jointly with Moscow and shared
with Paris, Warsaw and Dublin at the same hour, because whoever this is has now attacked two nuclear
powers and every capital at that table is a future target. The mole hunt continues on paper to its 
conclusion; no arrest, no interview, nothing that tips them, until the technical profile and the 
access list can be laid over each other. At home the Home Secretary gets what she needs to hold the 
streets - visible policing, the vigilante groups spoken to firmly and early, and daily truth in 
plain language, because a frightened country that trusts its government is governable and a 
frightened country that does not is the adversary's next weapon. And to Moscow: I will meet their 
President, in Dublin, in public, when we have a name to put on the table - not before, but I want 
them to know the offer stands. Whoever built this crisis wanted our two flags on opposite sides of 
it. I intend to hand them a photograph they cannot survive

Decision>: I have spent a week building a coalition abroad while my own country came apart behind 
me, and that stops tonight. The domestic emergency is now the main effort. The Home Secretary gets

fearing it every hour. The vigilante groups are met by their local chief constables in person 
tomorrow, with a simple message: your fear is legitimate, your patrols are not, and here is the 
number that reaches a real officer. And I go on television tonight - not a statement, an interview, 
hostile questions taken live - because a country that has been told a hijacked missile was aimed at 
it deserves to see whether its Prime Minister flinches. On the mole: nothing changes, the watch 
continues, and if name one's fragment moves we take them quietly and we take them alive. Everything 
I have built abroad is worth nothing if the state cannot keep the lights on and the peace at home

  Attorney General

  International Law and State Responsibility

  ! As the Legal Advisor, my expertise lies in international
    law, state responsibility, and use of
    force. I will provide a concise and professional assessment,
    referencing past decisions and warnings when relevant.

  If a non-state actor is found to have committed the attack
  while impersonating a state, this would be considered a
  violation of international law. The concept of state
  responsibility would not directly apply, as the actor is not a
  state. However, the state from which the non-state actor operated or
  received support could potentially be held responsible under
  international law.

  * Key Factors:         + Attribution: Can the
  non-state actor's actions be attributed to a particular state or
  organization?         + State responsibility: Could the
  state from which the non-state actor operated be held responsible under
  international law?         + Use of force: Would a military
  response against the non-state actor or the supporting state be
  considered a use of force under international law?

  A country cannot go to war with a company in
  the classical sense, as companies are not subjects of international law.
  However, a state could take lawful measures against a
  company or non-state actor that has committed a violation of
  international law, such as economic sanctions or
  law enforcement actions.
